claim: Gjd2b is expressed at high levels in the cerebellum of larval zebrafish beginning at 4 dpf.
source: Gjd2b is expressed at high levels in the cerebellum of larval zebrafish beginning at 4 dpf, a stage at which cerebellar neurons have been specified but chemical synaptic connections are still forming (Bae et al., 2009; Jabeen and Thirumalai, 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Bae et al., 2009; Jabeen and Thirumalai, 2013) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: At 4 dpf, cerebellar neurons have been specified but chemical synaptic connections are still forming.
source: Gjd2b is expressed at high levels in the cerebellum of larval zebrafish beginning at 4 dpf, a stage at which cerebellar neurons have been specified but chemical synaptic connections are still forming (Bae et al., 2009; Jabeen and Thirumalai, 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bae et al., 2009 and Jabeen and Thirumalai, 2013

claim: Gjd2a/b puncta localized to PN cell membrane in their cell bodies and dendrites.
source: Using an antibody that recognizes both Gjd2a and Gjd2b, we confirmed that Gjd2a/b puncta localized to PN cell membrane in their cell bodies and dendrites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Injection of Gjd2b-MO into 1–4 cell stage embryos interferes with normal splicing of the gjd2b gene product, resulting in the inclusion of a 40 base intronic segment in the mature mRNA.
source: Injection of this splice blocking morpholino (Gjd2b-MO) into 1–4 cell stage embryos interferes with normal splicing of the gjd2b gene product, resulting in the inclusion of a 40 base intronic segment in the mature mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, left).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: The mis-spliced gene product was detected in 2 dpf and 5 dpf larvae.
source: The mis-spliced gene product was detected in 2 dpf and 5 dpf larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: The mis-spliced gjd2b mRNA contains a premature stop codon resulting in a putative truncated protein of 24 amino acid residues in the N-terminus.
source: and the sequence reveals a premature stop codon resulting in a putative truncated protein of 24 amino acid residues in the N-terminus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, right).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: Gjd2a/b immunoreactivity in the PN and molecular layers of the cerebellum is reduced in Gjd2b-MO larvae compared to uninjected larvae.
source: Gjd2a/b immunoreactivity in the PN and molecular layers of the cerebellum is reduced in Gjd2b-MO larvae compared to uninjected larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, Mann–Whitney test, p<0.001) confirming effective knockdown.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D

claim: Injection of a morpholino with a 5-base mismatch (CTRL) did not alter Gjd2a/b protein levels.
source: Injection of a morpholino with a 5-base mismatch (CTRL) did not alter Gjd2a/b protein levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E, Mann–Whitney test, p=0.14).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E

claim: mEPSCs in Gjd2b-MO morphants occurred less frequently than in uninjected larvae.
source: mEPSCs in morphants occurred less frequently than in uninjected larvae (Figure 1A), reflected as increased inter-event intervals in the morphants (Figure 1C, Mann–Whitney test, U = 37,285, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1A and 1C

claim: mEPSCs in Gjd2b-MO morphants showed a small increase in the peak amplitude.
source: mEPSCs in morphants also showed a small increase in the peak amplitude (Figure 1D, Mann–Whitney test, U = 25,537, p=0.002)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: mEPSCs in Gjd2b-MO morphants showed faster decay time constants.
source: and faster decay time constants (Figure 1B, F, Mann–Whitney test, U = 25,018, p=0.014).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B and 1F

claim: The increase in inter-event intervals of mEPSCs suggests that knocking down Gjd2b leads to a decrease in the density of synapses impinging on PNs.
source: The increase in inter-event intervals of mEPSCs suggests that knocking down Gjd2b leads to a decrease in the density of synapses impinging on PNs.
evidence: Inference based on the observed increase in inter-event intervals

claim: The single-nucleotide insertion in gjd2bncb215 caused a frame shift and insertion of a premature stop codon, with a predicted truncated protein of 55 amino acid residues.
source: This single-nucleotide insertion caused a frame shift and insertion of a premature stop codon, with a predicted truncated protein of 55 amino acid residues (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: Homozygotes with the gjd2bncb215 mutation showed reduced Gjd2b-like immunoreactivity in their cerebellum.
source: Homozygotes with this mutation showed reduced Gjd2b-like immunoreactivity in their cerebellum (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2E and 2F

claim: The input resistance of gjd2b-/- mutant neurons was significantly higher compared to wild type when recorded with cesium gluconate internal solution.
source: These recordings were performed with cesium gluconate internal solution, and under these conditions, the input resistance of mutant neurons was significantly higher compared to wild type (WT; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: gjd2b-/- larvae showed a significant increase in mEPSC inter-event intervals.
source: gjd2b-/- larvae showed a significant increase in mEPSC inter-event intervals (Figure 3A, C, Mann–Whitney test, U = 4906, p=0.02), recapitulating the results observed after knock down of Gjd2b with Gjd2b-MO (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A and 3C

claim: gjd2b-/- homozygous mutants showed an increase in mEPSC peak amplitudes.
source: Further, homozygous mutants also showed an increase in peak amplitudes (Figure 3A, B, D, Mann–Whitney test, U = 3385, p<0.0001)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A, 3B, and 3D

claim: gjd2b-/- homozygous mutants showed faster kinetics as revealed by decreases in rise times.
source: and faster kinetics as revealed by decreases in rise times (Figure 3B, E, Mann–Whitney test, U = 2322, p<0.0001)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B and 3E

claim: gjd2b-/- homozygous mutants showed faster kinetics as revealed by decreases in decay time constants.
source: and decay time constants (Figure 3B, F, Mann–Whitney test, U = 2791, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B and 3F

claim: The results from gjd2b-/- mutants are consistent with the results obtained after knocking down Gjd2b with Gjd2b-MO and point to a decrease in the number of glutamatergic synaptic contacts impinging on PNs.
source: These results are consistent with the results obtained after knocking down Gjd2b with Gjd2b-MO and point to a decrease in the number of glutamatergic synaptic contacts impinging on PNs.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of morpholino and mutant data

claim: No NMDAR-mediated component of the evoked EPSC was recorded in PNs.
source: As is the case in developing mammalian PNs (Piochon et al., 2007), we recorded no NMDAR-mediated component of the evoked EPSC in PNs (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4B and citation to Piochon et al., 2007

claim: No current response was observed after application of NMDA in PNs held at −20 mV in the presence of TTX.
source: No current response was observed after application of NMDA (Figure 4C), suggesting the absence of NMDARs on PNs in 7 dpf zebrafish larvae.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C

claim: NMDARs are absent on PNs in 7 dpf zebrafish larvae.
source: No current response was observed after application of NMDA (Figure 4C), suggesting the absence of NMDARs on PNs in 7 dpf zebrafish larvae.
evidence: Inference based on lack of NMDA-evoked currents

claim: The CF-PN synapse shows paired pulse depression when pulses are placed 35 ms apart.
source: The CF-PN synapse shows paired pulse depression when pulses are placed 35 ms apart (Figure 4D, F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4D and 4F

claim: The PPR varied as a function of the ISI but did not vary significantly between the uninjected and Gjd2b-MO groups.
source: We tested a range of inter-stimulus intervals (ISIs) from 30 ms till 550 ms (in morphants) and till 1000 ms (in mutants) and found that the PPR varied as a function of the ISI but did not vary significantly between the uninjected and Gjd2b-MO groups (Figure 4E, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F = 3.979, df = 1, p=0.081)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4E

claim: The PPR did not vary significantly between WT and gjd2b-/- groups.
source: or WT and gjd2b-/- groups (Figures 4G, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, F = 2.039, df = 1, p=0.17).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G

claim: Knocking down or knocking out Gjd2b leads to a decrease in the number of glutamatergic synapses impinging on PNs.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that knocking down or knocking out Gjd2b leads to a decrease in the number of glutamatergic synapses impinging on PNs.
evidence: Inference based on multiple lines of electrophysiological evidence

claim: The density of synapses per cubic micrometer was significantly lower in gjd2b-/- larvae compared to WT larvae.
source: We found that the density of synapses per cubic micrometer was significantly lower in gjd2b-/- larvae compared to WT larvae (Figure 5B, E, Mann–Whitney test, U = 86,268, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B and 5E

claim: The distribution of synapse maturation indices was not different between WT and mutant larvae.
source: The distribution of synapse maturation indices was not different between WT and mutant larvae (Figure 5D, F, Mann–Whitney test, U = 4922, p=0.12).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D and 5F

claim: Gjd2b is involved in the formation of synapses in the molecular layer of the cerebellum.
source: In sum, these results indicate that Gjd2b is involved in the formation of synapses in the molecular layer of the cerebellum, to which PNs significantly contribute, but once formed, the maturation of synapses is independent of Gjd2b.
evidence: Inference based on synapse density data

claim: Once formed, the maturation of synapses is independent of Gjd2b.
source: In sum, these results indicate that Gjd2b is involved in the formation of synapses in the molecular layer of the cerebellum, to which PNs significantly contribute, but once formed, the maturation of synapses is independent of Gjd2b.
evidence: Inference based on synapse maturation index data

claim: An increase in peak amplitude combined with faster kinetics of mEPSCs in gjd2b-/- mutants suggested that synapses are placed electrotonically closer to the soma in mutant PNs than in WT larvae.
source: An increase in peak amplitude combined with faster kinetics of mEPSCs in gjd2b-/- mutants (Figure 3) suggested that synapses are placed electrotonically closer to the soma in mutant PNs than in WT larvae.
evidence: Inference based on electrophysiological properties

claim: Input resistance measured with potassium gluconate internal solution did not reveal any difference between WT and mutant PNs.
source: In addition, input resistance measured with potassium gluconate internal solution did not reveal any difference between WT and mutant PNs
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Recordings with cesium gluconate showed that the input resistance was higher for mutant PNs compared to WT.
source: while recordings with cesium gluconate showed that the input resistance was higher for mutant PNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Loss of Gjd2b could result in stunted dendritic arbors and loss of distally located synapses.
source: These data imply that loss of Gjd2b could result in stunted dendritic arbors and loss of distally located synapses.
evidence: Inference based on electrophysiological and input resistance data

claim: WT PNs showed a significant increase in their TDBL from 5 dpf to 6 dpf, but not at later stages.
source: WT PNs showed a significant increase in their TDBL from 5 dpf to 6 dpf, but not at later stages (Figure 6C, generalized linear model [GLM], 5 dpf vs. 6 dpf difference estimate = –2.26e-05, 95% CI = −3.84e-05 to −6.68e-06, z ratio = –3.357, p=0.002; 6 dpf vs. 7 dpf difference estimate = –9.73e-06, 95% CI = –2.25e-05 to 3.00e-06, z ratio = –1.806, p=0.1821; 7 dpf vs. 8 dpf difference estimate = –1.48e-06, 95% CI = −1.35e-05 to 1.05e-05, z ratio = –0.291, p=0.98).
evidence: Supported by imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: gjd2b-/- PNs showed a similar pattern of branch length growth to WT, with an increase in TDBL from 5 to 6 dpf, followed by no significant increase until 8 dpf.
source: gjd2b-/- PNs also showed a similar pattern of branch length growth, with an increase in TDBL from 5 to 6 dpf, followed by no significant increase until 8 dpf (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C

claim: There was a significant difference in TDBL between WT and gjd2b-/- on all 4 days, with the mutant group having consistently lower values.
source: Post-hoc analysis revealed that there was a significant difference in TDBL between WT and gjd2b-/- on all 4 days, with the mutant group having consistently lower values (Figure 6A–C, GLM, WT vs. mutant difference estimate = 8.17e-06, z ratio = 1.974, p=0.048).
evidence: Supported by imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6A-C

claim: PN somata in WT and gjd2b-/- larvae were comparable in diameter.
source: PN somata in WT and gjd2b-/- larvae were comparable in diameter (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, linear model, WT vs. mutant difference estimate = 0.3227, t = 1.935, p=0.055).
evidence: Supported by imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: Loss of Gjd2b leads to a stunted dendritic arbor having fewer synapses.
source: These analyses reveal that loss of Gjd2b leads to a stunted dendritic arbor having fewer synapses.
evidence: Inference based on dendritic morphology and synapse density data

claim: Since the arbor is stunted in mutants, the synapses that are present on the arbor are electrically closer to the soma compared to WT.
source: Since the arbor is stunted in mutants, the synapses that are present on the arbor are electrically closer to the soma compared to WT.
evidence: Inference based on dendritic morphology data

claim: The electrically closer location of synapses in mutants may lead to the increased amplitudes and faster kinetics of mEPSCs recorded from the soma.
source: This may in turn lead to the increased amplitudes and faster kinetics of mEPSCs recorded from the soma.
evidence: Inference based on electrophysiological and morphological data

claim: WT neurons showed a significant increase in branch numbers from 6 dpf to 7 dpf, but not at any other stages.
source: WT neurons showed a significant increase in branch numbers from 6 dpf to 7 dpf, but not at any other stages (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, GLM with Poisson error distribution, 5 dpf vs. 6 dpf ratio = 1.132, z ratio = 2.175, p=0.0797; 6 dpf vs. 7 dpf ratio = 1.166, z ratio = 2.862, p=0.012; 7 dpf vs. 8 dpf ratio = 0.949, z ratio = –0.985, p=0.65).
evidence: Supported by imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: gjd2b-/- PNs showed a similar pattern of branch number growth to WT, with an increase in TDBN from 6 to 7 dpf, followed by no significant increase until 8 dpf.
source: gjd2b-/- PNs also showed a similar pattern of branch number growth, with an increase in TDBN from 6 to 7 dpf, followed by no significant increase until 8 dpf (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: There was a significant difference in TDBN between WT and gjd2b-/- on all 4 days, with the mutant group having consistently higher values.
source: Post-hoc analysis revealed that there was a significant difference in TDBN between WT and gjd2b-/- on all 4 days, with the mutant group having consistently higher values (GLM with Poisson error distribution, WT vs. mutant ratio = 1.16, z ratio = 3.708, p=0.0002).
evidence: Supported by imaging data and statistical analysis

claim: WT and mutant neurons did not show any difference in the branching order at 7 dpf, as analyzed by Sholl analysis.
source: Despite these differences, WT and mutant neurons did not show any difference in the branching order at 7 dpf, as analyzed by Sholl analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, linear mixed model, WT vs. mutant difference estimate = –0.003208, z = –0.115, p=0.91).
evidence: Supported by Sholl analysis data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: Mutant neurons had a significantly reduced growth rate compared to WT PNs.
source: Mutant neurons had a significantly reduced growth rate compared to WT PNs (Figure 6D, linear model, WT vs. mutant difference estimate = 0.025462, t = 2.777, p=0.006).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: Mutant neurons had a significantly lower rate of branch elongations than WT neurons.
source: When dissected further into branch elongations and retractions, mutant neurons had a significantly lower rate of branch elongations than WT neurons (Figure 6E, linear model, WT vs. mutant difference estimate = 0.015030, t = 2.307, p=0.022)
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6E

claim: Mutant neurons' rates of branch length retractions were similar to WT neurons.
source: but their rates of branch length retractions were similar (Figure 6F, WT vs. mutant difference estimate = 0.009621, t = 1.33, p=0.185).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6F

claim: Gjd2b regulates dendritic growth by promoting branch elongations and is unlikely to be involved in regulating branch retractions.
source: This suggests that Gjd2b regulates dendritic growth by promoting branch elongations and is unlikely to be involved in regulating branch retractions.
evidence: Inference based on differential effects on elongation vs. retraction

claim: When non-PNs were electroporated with neurobiotin or serotonin, one or two PNs along with several non-PNs were detected.
source: However, when non-PNs were electroporated with neurobiotin or serotonin, one or two PNs along with several non-PNs were detected (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Supported by electroporation and dye coupling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1

claim: PNs are likely to be coupled to other cerebellar cell types via rectifying junctions.
source: indicating that PNs are likely to be coupled to other cerebellar cell types via rectifying junctions.
evidence: Inference based on dye coupling patterns

claim: TDBL in mutant PNs expressing Gjd2b were significantly larger than mutant PNs and were rescued to WT levels.
source: TDBL in mutant PNs expressing Gjd2b were significantly larger than mutant PNs and were rescued to WT levels (Figure 7B, ANOVA post-hoc Tukey HSD, difference estimate = –74.6, t-ratio = –5.336, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B

claim: The presence of Gjd2b in single PNs in otherwise Gjd2b null larvae is sufficient to guide dendritic arbor elongation.
source: This suggests that the presence of Gjd2b in single PNs in otherwise Gjd2b null larvae is sufficient to guide dendritic arbor elongation.
evidence: Inference based on rescue experiment results

claim: Expression of Gjd2bΔ5-21 in PNs of gjd2b-/- larvae resulted in dendritic arbors that remained stunted and not significantly larger than mutant PNs lacking Gjd2b.
source: Expression of Gjd2bΔ5-21 in PNs of gjd2b-/- larvae resulted in dendritic arbors that remained stunted and not significantly larger than mutant PNs lacking Gjd2b (Figure 7B, ANOVA post-hoc Tukey HSD, difference estimate = –18.5, t-ratio = –1.506, p=0.4370).
evidence: Supported by imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B

claim: Functional gap junctional channels are required for regulating PN dendritic elaboration.
source: These results point to the need for functional gap junctional channels in regulating PN dendritic elaboration.
evidence: Inference based on pore-dead mutant rescue experiment

claim: Dendritic branches having at least one Gjd2b punctum elongated more in length during the 5 min observation windows compared to branches that did not possess any puncta.
source: Dendritic branches having at least one Gjd2b punctum elongated more in length during the 5 min observation windows compared to branches that did not possess any puncta (Mann–Whitney test, U = 3779.5, p=0.022).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data and statistical analysis

claim: Presence of Gjd2b puncta did not affect branch retraction lengths.
source: Presence of Gjd2b puncta did not affect branch retraction lengths during the same window (Figure 7C, Mann–Whitney test, U = 4048, p=0.098).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7C

claim: Functional Gjd2b promotes the elongation of dendritic branches on which it is present.
source: In sum, these results show that functional Gjd2b promotes the elongation of dendritic branches on which it is present.
evidence: Inference based on branch-level imaging data

claim: CaMKII has been shown to associate with Cx35/36-mediated gap junctions and modulate their function.
source: The calcium and calmodulin-dependent kinase II (CaMKII) has been shown to associate with Cx35/36-mediated gap junctions and modulate their function (Pereda et al., 1998; Alev et al., 2008; Flores et al., 2010; Tetenborg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: CaMKII is localized in dendrites and in spines and is a critical regulator of dendritic development.
source: CaMKII is localized in dendrites and in spines and is a critical regulator of dendritic development (Wu and Cline, 1998; Zou and Cline, 1999; Wayman et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Increased copy numbers for all isoforms of camk2 tested were observed in gjd2b-/- compared to WT.
source: To our surprise, we observed increased copy numbers for all isoforms of camk2 we tested in gjd2b-/- compared to WT (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 7D

claim: CaMKII has previously been shown to reduce dendritic dynamics and stabilize branches.
source: CaMKII has previously been shown to reduce dendritic dynamics and stabilize branches (Wu and Cline, 1998; Zou and Cline, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Incubation in KN-93 was able to rescue dendritic arbor lengths of PNs in gjd2b-/- larvae to WT levels.
source: Incubation in KN-93 was able to rescue dendritic arbor lengths of PNs in gjd2b-/- larvae to WT levels (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data and pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 7E

claim: No changes in dendritic arbor lengths were observed in larvae incubated in DMSO (vehicle control) or in KN-92, an inactive analog of KN-93.
source: No changes in dendritic arbor lengths were observed in larvae incubated in DMSO (vehicle control) or in KN-92, an inactive analog of KN-93 (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data and pharmacological controls shown in Figure 7E

claim: Conduction via Gjd2b-mediated electrical synapses is critical for proper glutamatergic synaptogenesis in PNs.
source: Taken together, these results show that conduction via Gjd2b-mediated electrical synapses is critical for proper glutamatergic synaptogenesis in PNs and that this process affects dendritic arbor growth.
evidence: Inference based on multiple lines of evidence from rescue and pharmacological experiments

claim: Conduction via Gjd2b-mediated electrical synapses affects dendritic arbor growth.
source: Taken together, these results show that conduction via Gjd2b-mediated electrical synapses is critical for proper glutamatergic synaptogenesis in PNs and that this process affects dendritic arbor growth.
evidence: Inference based on multiple lines of evidence from rescue and pharmacological experiments

claim: Cx36, the mammalian homolog of Gjd2b, has been shown to be expressed in the rodent cerebellar cortex in the molecular layer and granule cell layer.
source: Cx36, the mammalian homolog of Gjd2b, has been shown to be expressed in the rodent cerebellar cortex in the molecular layer and granule cell layer (Belluardo et al., 2000; Degen et al., 2004; Nagy and Rash, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Cx36 puncta were observed localized to PNs.
source: and Cx36 puncta were observed localized to PNs (Alcami and Marty, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Alcami and Marty, 2013

claim: Cx36 mRNA was not found in PNs.
source: although the mRNA was not found in PNs (Belluardo et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Belluardo et al., 2000

claim: In larval zebrafish, cell type-specific transcriptome analysis revealed gjd2b expression in PNs, granule cells, eurydendroid cells, and Bergmann glial cells.
source: In larval zebrafish, cell type-specific transcriptome analysis in larval zebrafish revealed gjd2b expression in PNs, granule cells, eurydendroid cells, and Bergmann glial cells (Takeuchi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takeuchi et al., 2017

claim: Zebrafish Gjd2b channels have a unitary conductance of around 24 pS.
source: This may be attributable to the low conductance of zebrafish Gjd2b channels, which have a unitary conductance of around 24 pS (Valiunas et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Valiunas et al., 2004

claim: Cx36 channels have very small unitary conductances of 10–15 pS.
source: This is also true of Cx36, which have very small unitary conductances of 10–15 pS (Srinivas et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Srinivas et al., 1999

claim: Cx36 has been shown to not support dye coupling.
source: Cx36 has been shown to not support dye coupling (Teubner et al., 2000; Quesada et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Teubner et al., 2000 and Quesada et al., 2003

claim: When cells were made to overexpress Cx32, which has a larger conductance compared to Cx36, dye coupling could be observed.
source: Further, when these same cells were made to overexpress Cx32, which has a larger conductance compared to Cx36, dye coupling could be observed (Quesada et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Quesada et al., 2003

claim: Electrical coupling in the absence of dye coupling has been widely observed.
source: Electrical coupling in the absence of dye coupling has been widely observed (Ransom and Kettenmann, 1990; Meda et al., 1991; Pérez-Armendariz et al., 1991; Moser, 1998; Teubner et al., 2000; Quesada et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: PNs in fish and mammals are electrically coupled to other neurons, likely mediated by Cx36 in mammals and Cx35 in zebrafish.
source: From these studies, it appears that PNs in fish and mammals are electrically coupled to other neurons, likely mediated by Cx36 in mammals and Cx35 in zebrafish.
evidence: Inference based on literature review and current findings

claim: Gap junctions on PNs could serve important developmental functions in all vertebrates.
source: We suggest that these gap junctions on PNs could serve important developmental functions in all vertebrates.
evidence: Speculation based on comparative analysis

claim: Knockdown of the innexin inx1 in leech resulted in loss of electrical coupling between identified neurons at embryonic stages and decreased chemical synaptic strength between the same neurons at much later stages.
source: Knockdown of the innexin inx1 in leech resulted in loss of electrical coupling between identified neurons at embryonic stages and decreased chemical synaptic strength between the same neurons at much later stages (Todd et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Todd et al., 2010

claim: In the neocortex of mice, sister neurons born from the same radial glia make transient electrical synapses, which are required for the formation of excitatory connections between them.
source: In the neocortex of mice, sister neurons born from the same radial glia make transient electrical synapses, which are required for the formation of excitatory connections between them (Yu et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yu et al., 2009 and Yu et al., 2012

claim: Mice lacking Cx36 exhibit reduced synaptic connectivity between mitral cells in the olfactory bulb.
source: Mice lacking Cx36 exhibit reduced synaptic connectivity between mitral cells in the olfactory bulb (Maher et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maher et al., 2009

claim: An increase in the number of inhibitory synapses was observed in Cx36-/- mice in thalamocortical relay neurons with a concomitant decrease in their dendritic complexity.
source: However, an increase in the number of inhibitory synapses was observed in Cx36-/- mice in thalamocortical relay neurons with a concomitant decrease in their dendritic complexity (Zolnik and Connors, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zolnik and Connors, 2016

claim: In rodents, lack of afferent input during the second postnatal week results in abnormal orientation, reduced size, and lack of higher-order branches in PN dendritic arbors.
source: In rodents, lack of afferent input during this phase results in abnormal orientation, reduced size, and lack of higher-order branches in PN dendritic arbors (Altman and Anderson, 1972; Rakic and Sidman, 1973).
evidence: Supported by citations to Altman and Anderson, 1972 and Rakic and Sidman, 1973

claim: In both slice cultures and dissociated cell cultures, blockade of glutamatergic transmission reduces dendritic arbor size of PNs.
source: In both slice cultures and dissociated cell cultures, blockade of glutamatergic transmission reduces dendritic arbor size of PNs (Catania et al., 2001; Adcock et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Catania et al., 2001 and Adcock et al., 2004

claim: It is likely that the reduced glutamatergic synapses in gjd2b-/- PNs lead to a stunted dendritic arbor via a synaptotrophic mechanism.
source: It is likely that the reduced glutamatergic synapses in gjd2b-/- PNs lead to a stunted dendritic arbor via a synaptotrophic mechanism (Haas et al., 2006; Cline and Haas, 2008).
evidence: Speculation supported by citations to Haas et al., 2006 and Cline and Haas, 2008

claim: In Xenopus tectum, immature neurons with simple arbors and low levels of CaMKII continue to grow while mature neurons have high levels of CaMKII and their dendritic structure is more or less stable.
source: In Xenopus tectum, immature neurons with simple arbors and low levels of CaMKII continue to grow while mature neurons have high levels of CaMKII and their dendritic structure is more or less stable.
evidence: Draws from established findings in Xenopus tectum
